title: Red flag: chest pain or pressure
content: Chest pain, tightness, pressure or heaviness in the chest, especially with sweating, nausea, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back, can be a heart attack. This is an emergency: call emergency services immediately. Do not drive yourself. Chew aspirin only if not allergic and not advised otherwise. Heart symptoms are worse with exertion and may improve with rest.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: stroke signs — FAST
content: Signs of a stroke: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness on one side, Speech difficulty or confusion. Time is critical — call emergency services immediately if any of these appear suddenly. Also note sudden severe headache with no known cause, sudden vision loss, or trouble walking as possible stroke signs.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: anaphylaxis
content: Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergic reaction. Signs: trouble breathing or wheezing, swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, hives with difficulty swallowing, dizziness or collapse, and a fast heartbeat. This is an emergency — call emergency services and use an epinephrine auto-injector immediately if available. Anaphylaxis can follow food, insect stings, or medication.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: severe difficulty breathing
content: Breathing that is so hard the patient cannot finish a sentence, blue or grey lips or fingertips, gasping, or a sudden inability to breathe requires immediate emergency care. In children, look for sucking in of the chest wall between the ribs or flaring of the nostrils with each breath.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: severe bleeding
content: Bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of firm direct pressure, or blood that soaks through a dressing and keeps flowing, is an emergency. So does coughing up or vomiting blood, or black tarry stools, which suggest internal bleeding. Call emergency services and keep pressure on the wound.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: head injury with confusion
content: After a head injury, seek emergency care if the person loses consciousness, is confused, vomits more than once, has a severe or worsening headache, unequal pupils, seizures, or weakness on one side. Also urgent for infants, older adults, or people on blood thinners after any head bump. Simple concussions without these signs still need a medical check.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: severe abdominal pain
content: Sudden, severe or worsening abdominal pain — especially with fever, vomiting, a rigid or tender abdomen, blood in stool, or pain that moves to the lower right side — can indicate appendicitis, gallstones, or other emergencies. Emergency care is needed. Severe abdominal pain in pregnancy is always urgent.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: fever in infants under 3 months
content: Any fever (temperature at or above 100.4 F / 38 C) in a baby under 3 months old is an emergency — the baby's immune system is immature and serious infections can develop fast. Call emergency services or go to urgent care/ER immediately. Do not self-treat with fever medicine first.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: severe dehydration
content: Severe dehydration signs: no urine for 8+ hours (or no wet diaper in 6 hours in a child), sunken eyes or fontanelle (soft spot), extreme thirst, dry mouth with little saliva, dizziness on standing, confusion, or rapid heart rate. This needs urgent medical care, possibly IV fluids. Mild dehydration can be treated at home with oral rehydration.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: seizures
content: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, a first-ever seizure, difficulty breathing after a seizure, or a seizure in pregnancy is an emergency — call emergency services. During a seizure, protect the person from injury, do not hold them down, and do not put anything in their mouth.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: confusion or altered consciousness
content: Sudden confusion, disorientation, drowsiness that is hard to wake from, or fainting, especially in an older adult or someone with diabetes, warrants urgent evaluation — it can signal stroke, low blood sugar, infection, or other serious causes. Check blood sugar in a diabetic and give fast sugar if low, but seek urgent care regardless.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: high fever with stiff neck
content: Fever together with a stiff neck, severe headache, rash that does not blanch when pressed, sensitivity to light, or confusion can be meningitis. This is an emergency. The rash plus fever combination (meningococcal) needs same-day emergency evaluation even without other signs.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: thoughts of self-harm
content: Any thoughts of harming oneself or suicide are an emergency. Stay with the person, remove dangerous items, and call emergency services or a crisis line immediately. Take all statements about self-harm seriously, even if the person seems calm.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: poisoning or overdose
content: Suspected poisoning, overdose, or ingestion of medicines not meant for the person (especially children) is urgent — call emergency services or poison control immediately. Do not induce vomiting unless a professional tells you to. Bring the suspected substance container with you.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Red flag: burns
content: Seek emergency care for burns that are deep, larger than the palm of the hand, on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a major joint, or caused by electricity or chemicals. Cool the burn under running water for 10-20 minutes first. Never apply ice, butter, oil or toothpaste. Minor first-degree burns heal at home with cool water and moisturizer.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: fever in adults
content: For a mild fever (below 39 C / 102.2 F) in an otherwise healthy adult: rest, drink plenty of fluids, and use paracetamol or ibuprofen following the package dose if uncomfortable. Dress lightly, do not bundle up. See a doctor if the fever lasts more than 3 days, keeps rising above 39.4 C / 103 F, or comes with severe symptoms. Paracetamol and ibuprofen can be alternated but must not be taken in overdose.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: cold compress and ice
content: For sprains, strains, and minor swelling: apply a cold pack wrapped in a thin cloth for 15-20 minutes at a time, several times a day, for the first 48 hours. After 48 hours, gentle heat can help. Rest the injured part and elevate it above heart level to reduce swelling. See a doctor if you cannot bear weight, or swelling worsens after 2-3 days.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: hydration
content: Aim for roughly 6-8 glasses of water a day; more in heat, exercise, fever, or vomiting and diarrhea. Urine color is a practical guide — pale yellow means well hydrated. For mild vomiting or diarrhea, take small frequent sips of an oral rehydration solution (water with a pinch of salt and a spoon of sugar) rather than large amounts at once.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: sore throat gargle
content: A warm salt-water gargle (half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water) several times a day soothes a sore throat. Honey in warm water or tea also helps a cough and sore throat in adults and children over 1 year. Lozenges, fluids, and rest speed recovery. See a doctor for severe pain, difficulty swallowing saliva, a muffled voice, or a sore throat lasting over a week.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: minor wound care
content: For minor cuts and scrapes: wash your hands, rinse the wound under clean running water, gently clean around it with soap, apply firm pressure with a clean cloth for a few minutes to stop bleeding, then cover with a sterile dressing. Change the dressing daily and watch for signs of infection: increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or red streaks — that needs a doctor.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: food poisoning and stomach upset
content: For mild food poisoning or gastroenteritis: rest the stomach, sip fluids frequently, and eat bland foods (rice, bananas, toast, plain crackers) when you feel ready. Avoid dairy, fatty, spicy, and sugary foods for a few days. Most cases settle in 24-48 hours. See a doctor for blood in stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of dehydration.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: back pain
content: For simple back pain, stay as active as pain allows — prolonged bed rest makes it worse. Apply heat for muscle spasm and gentle stretching. Use paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed. Most back pain improves within 2-4 weeks. Urgent if there is leg weakness, numbness in the groin, loss of bladder or bowel control, or pain after a fall or injury.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: insect stings
content: For bee or wasp stings: scrape out any visible stinger with a fingernail or credit card (do not squeeze it), wash the area, apply a cold pack, and take an antihistamine for itching. Watch for signs of a severe allergic reaction — breathing trouble, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness — which is an emergency.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: sunburn
content: For sunburn: cool the skin with a cool shower or compresses, apply a fragrance-free moisturizer or aloe, drink extra fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain. Avoid further sun exposure. Seek medical care for severe blistering over a large area, fever, chills, or dizziness, which suggest sun poisoning or dehydration.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: sleep hygiene
content: Good sleep basics: keep a regular sleep-wake schedule, a cool dark quiet bedroom, avoid screens 30-60 minutes before bed, avoid caffeine after mid-afternoon, and get natural daylight in the morning. Limit naps to 20-30 minutes. Chronic insomnia (several weeks) or loud snoring with daytime sleepiness may need a medical review for sleep apnea.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: nausea without vomiting
content: For mild nausea: eat small bland meals, sip ginger tea or lemon water, avoid strong smells and fatty food, and get fresh air. Ginger and peppermint can help. Seek medical care for nausea with severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting for more than a day, vomiting blood, or signs of dehydration.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: ear pain
content: For mild ear discomfort: apply a warm compress, rest upright, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen. Avoid putting anything in the ear. See a doctor for severe pain, fever, discharge from the ear, hearing loss, or ear pain in a child under 2, or pain that lasts more than 2-3 days.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Self-care: eye irritation
content: For mild eye redness or irritation: rinse with clean saline, use artificial tears, and avoid rubbing the eye. Cold compresses help allergy eyes. See a doctor urgently for eye pain, vision changes, light sensitivity, a foreign body that will not rinse out, or green/yellow discharge that sticks the lids together.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: what counts as a fever
content: A fever is generally a temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher. Normal body temperature is about 98.6 F (37 C) and varies through the day, lowest in the morning. How high the fever goes matters less than how the person looks and feels: a fever is not dangerous by itself and helps the body fight infection. Focus on comfort, fluids, and the person's overall condition.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: when to treat with medicine
content: Treat fever medicine for comfort, not for the number on the thermometer. In adults, treat if fever causes discomfort — paracetamol (acetaminophen) every 4-6 hours or ibuprofen every 6-8 hours, never exceeding the maximum daily dose. Do not give aspirin to children or teenagers (Reye's syndrome risk). Follow weight-based dosing for children and the package instructions for adults.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: child fever care
content: For a child over 3 months with fever: keep them comfortable, offer fluids often, and use paracetamol (or ibuprofen over 6 months) at the correct weight-based dose. Dress the child lightly. Seek care if the fever lasts over 3 days, the child is very lethargic, not drinking, has trouble breathing, has a rash, or is in pain. Febrile seizures (shaking during a fast-rising fever) usually pass safely, but always get the child checked afterward.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: hydration during fever
content: Fevers increase fluid loss, so drink more than usual: water, clear soups, oral rehydration solutions, or diluted juice. Signs of dehydration during fever include dark urine, dry mouth, and dizziness. In babies, fewer wet diapers than usual. Seek urgent care if fluid intake is impossible or dehydration signs appear.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: fever with rash
content: A fever with a rash can be harmless (viral rashes, roseola) or serious. A rash of small dark red or purple spots that do not fade when pressed with a glass can be meningitis — emergency. A fever with hives can be an allergic reaction. Fever with chickenpox brings itchy blisters that crust over. When in doubt, get a fever-plus-rash evaluated the same day.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: how long a fever can last
content: Most viral fevers last 2-3 days, some up to a week. The pattern matters: fevers that come and go for more than 3 days, return after a few days of being well, or are accompanied by new severe symptoms need a medical review. A fever that comes and goes with chills, sweats, and weight loss deserves prompt evaluation.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: temperature taking
content: Rectal thermometers are most accurate in babies and young children. Oral (under the tongue) works for children over 4 and adults. Ear thermometers are convenient but less accurate. Axillary (armpit) readings run about 1 degree F (0.5 C) lower. Wait 30 minutes after eating or exercise before measuring.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: fever with chills and body aches
content: Fever with chills and body aches is common in flu, viral infections, and sometimes bacterial infections. Chills mean the body is raising its temperature. Warm clothing and blankets during chills are fine; remove layers once the fever breaks. Body aches usually settle within a few days with rest, fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen. See a doctor if they worsen or persist beyond 5 days.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Fever: infant fever 3-6 months
content: In babies 3-6 months old, a fever of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher should be checked by a doctor the same day, even if the baby seems well, because serious infections are harder to spot at this age. Between 6 months and 2 years, a fever lasting over 24 hours, or any fever with poor feeding, lethargy, or unusual crying, needs a check.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: cold vs flu
content: The common cold comes on gradually with sneezing, runny nose, and mild sore throat, rarely with significant fever. The flu comes on suddenly with high fever, chills, severe body aches, headache, and fatigue, with cough later. COVID-19 can look like either, often adding loss of smell or taste. Rest, fluids and symptom relief help both; antibiotics do not treat viral infections.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: flu warning signs
content: See a doctor promptly if flu symptoms include difficulty breathing, chest pain or pressure, confusion, severe weakness, dehydration, a fever that lasts more than 3 days, or symptoms that improve then suddenly worsen. Antiviral flu medicines work best when started within the first 48 hours, especially for high-risk groups.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: common cold self-care
content: For a common cold: rest, warm fluids, honey for cough, saline nasal spray or steam for congestion, and paracetamol for aches and fever. Colds typically peak at 2-3 days and clear within 7-10 days. Green mucus alone does not mean antibiotics are needed. Seek care for symptoms lasting over 10 days, high fever, or worsening after a week.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: nasal congestion relief
content: For stuffy nose: saline nasal sprays or drops, steam inhalation (careful with hot water), and keeping the head elevated at night help. In infants, a rubber-bulb suction after saline drops clears the nose before feeds. Decongestant sprays should not be used for more than 3 days. Sinus pain or green discharge lasting over 10 days suggests sinusitis needing a doctor.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: cough basics
content: Most coughs from colds last 1-3 weeks and are caused by irritation, not infection of the lungs. Honey (over 1 year old), warm drinks, and lozenges help. See a doctor for a cough lasting more than 3 weeks, coughing up blood, high fever, chest pain, difficulty breathing, or a cough that comes with weight loss. A dry cough plus breathlessness can be a sign of asthma or other lung conditions.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: sore throat causes
content: Most sore throats are viral and clear in a week with fluids, rest, and pain relief. Strep throat (bacterial) is more likely with severe pain, fever over 38 C, tender neck glands, and NO cough or runny nose — a doctor can do a rapid test and prescribe antibiotics only if positive. Untreated strep can rarely cause rheumatic fever, so check severe cases.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: antibiotics and viruses
content: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Colds, flu, most sore throats, and most coughs and sinus infections are viral, so antibiotics will not help and can cause side effects and resistance. Complete the full course when antibiotics ARE prescribed. Ask your doctor when treatment is unclear rather than demanding antibiotics.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: flu vaccine
content: Annual flu vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older, especially pregnant women, older adults, young children, and people with chronic conditions. The vaccine reduces flu risk and makes illness milder. It takes about 2 weeks to protect. Flu shots do not cause the flu.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: cold in babies
content: Babies get frequent colds. Keep them comfortable, offer feeds more often, and clear a blocked nose before feeds. See a doctor for any fever under 3 months, fever over 3 days, trouble breathing, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness, or cold symptoms lasting over 10 days. Cough and cold syrups are not recommended for children under 6.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Cold and flu: when flu needs urgent care
content: Go to urgent care or the ER for flu with: difficulty breathing or chest pain, confusion or not waking, severe dehydration (no urine, dizziness when standing), a fever above 40 C (104 F), seizures, or symptoms that improve then suddenly worsen — which can signal a secondary pneumonia. High-risk groups (elderly, pregnant, chronic illness) should seek care earlier.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: tension headache
content: Tension headaches feel like a tight band or pressure around the head, usually mild to moderate, and can last 30 minutes to days. Triggers include stress, poor posture, and screen time. Relief: paracetamol or ibuprofen, rest, neck stretches, hydration, and stress management. Overusing painkillers more than 2-3 days a week can itself cause rebound headaches.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: migraine basics
content: Migraine is a severe throbbing headache, often one-sided, with nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people see auras (flashing lights, zigzag lines) beforehand. Attacks last 4-72 hours. Quiet, dark rooms, sleep, fluids, and early medication help. Frequent migraines (4+ per month) deserve a medical review for preventive treatment.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: red flag thunderclap headache
content: A sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache that peaks within seconds to a minute — 'the worst headache of my life' — can be a brain bleed (subarachnoid hemorrhage). This is an emergency even if it fades. Also urgent: headache with fever and stiff neck, after a head injury, with weakness or confusion, with vision problems, or a new headache in someone over 50.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: sinus headache
content: Sinus headaches cause pressure and pain over the forehead, cheeks, or around the eyes, worse when bending forward, often with nasal congestion. They usually accompany a cold or sinusitis. Relief: steam, warm compresses, saline rinse, fluids, and paracetamol or ibuprofen. Persistent pain with green discharge over 10 days may be bacterial sinusitis needing a doctor.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: screen and posture headaches
content: Long screen time, poor posture, eye strain, and dehydration commonly trigger headaches. Relief: follow the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes look 20 feet away for 20 seconds), keep the screen at eye level, take breaks, and drink water. Persistent headaches that started after glasses are due or with eye pain deserve an eye check.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: caffeine headaches
content: Caffeine both treats and causes headaches: it can boost painkillers, but regular caffeine users get withdrawal headaches when they miss their usual intake — typically 12-24 hours after the last cup. Limit caffeine to a regular moderate amount, and taper rather than stopping abruptly. Headaches from skipping meals are common too; eat regularly.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Headache: when a headache needs a doctor
content: Make a doctor's appointment for headaches that: are new and persistent, come more than 15 days a month, change pattern, interrupt sleep, or come with vision changes, weakness, or numbness. Keep a headache diary (timing, triggers, medicine use) to bring along. Over-the-counter painkillers used more than 2-3 times a week can make headaches worse.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: what the numbers mean
content: Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic (e.g. 120/80). Normal is below 120/80. Elevated is 120-129/80. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is 130/80 or higher confirmed on repeated readings. One high reading is not a diagnosis — it should be checked again when relaxed. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, which is why it is called the silent killer; regular checks matter.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: home monitoring
content: For home BP monitoring: sit quietly for 5 minutes, feet flat, arm at heart level, cuff on bare upper arm, no smoking or caffeine 30 minutes before. Take two readings 1-2 minutes apart, morning and evening, for a week. Record all readings for your doctor. Home readings are usually lower than clinic readings — share your log.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: salt reduction
content: Cutting salt is one of the most effective non-drug ways to lower blood pressure. Aim under 5-6 g of salt (about one teaspoon) per day. Most salt is hidden in packaged food, pickles, sauces, cheese, and bread. Cook with herbs, spices, lemon, and garlic instead; read labels and choose low-sodium options; gradually your taste adapts.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: lifestyle measures
content: Blood pressure responds to: regular exercise (30 minutes most days), a diet rich in vegetables and fruit with less processed food, maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol (max 1-2 drinks a day), not smoking, sleeping 7-9 hours, and managing stress. These measures can prevent, delay, or reduce the need for medication.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: hypertensive urgency vs emergency
content: A very high reading (180/120 or higher) is a hypertensive crisis. If there are NO symptoms, recheck in 5 minutes and contact a doctor the same day. If there ARE symptoms — severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, vision changes, numbness or weakness, confusion — it is an emergency: call emergency services. Do not abruptly stop BP medicines without advice.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: medication adherence
content: Blood pressure medicines work only when taken regularly — usually at the same time daily. Missing doses allows pressure to climb silently. Never stop or halve doses because you 'feel fine'; that can cause dangerous rebound rises. Tell your doctor about dizziness or side effects so the dose can be adjusted rather than stopping on your own.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: symptoms of very high BP
content: High blood pressure itself rarely causes symptoms, but very high levels can cause severe headache, chest pain, visual disturbances, nausea, anxiety, confusion, or shortness of breath. Facial flushing alone is usually not high BP. Routine screening is the only reliable way to catch it early — everyone over 30 should know their numbers.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Hypertension: who needs treatment
content: Treatment decisions depend on your numbers, age, and other risks (diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, family history). Lifestyle changes are recommended for everyone; medicines are added when pressure stays high despite lifestyle, or immediately for very high readings or high-risk groups. Target is usually below 130/80 but your doctor individualizes it.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: type 1 vs type 2
content: Type 1 diabetes usually starts in children or young adults when the body stops making insulin — daily insulin injections are essential, forever. Type 2 diabetes is far more common, usually develops after 40, and is linked to weight, inactivity, and family history; it is managed with lifestyle, tablets, and sometimes insulin. Both need blood sugar control to prevent complications.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
content: Low blood sugar (below 70 mg/dL) causes sweating, shaking, hunger, fast heartbeat, confusion, and irritability; it can progress to unconsciousness. The 15-15 rule: eat 15 g of fast sugar (3-4 glucose tablets, 4 oz juice, or a tablespoon of honey), wait 15 minutes, recheck, and repeat if still low. Then eat a snack with protein. Severe hypoglycemia (unconscious, seizure) needs emergency help and glucagon if available. Always seek a review after any severe low.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: high blood sugar (hyperglycemia)
content: High blood sugar causes thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, blurred vision, and slow healing. Persistent levels well above target warrant adjusting treatment with your care team. Urgent danger signs: very high sugar with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, rapid deep breathing, confusion, or extreme thirst — these suggest ketoacidosis (type 1) or hyperosmolar state (type 2) and need emergency care.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: sick day rules
content: During illness: check blood sugar more often (every 3-4 hours), never skip diabetes medicines or insulin (sickness raises sugar), drink plenty of sugar-free fluids, and aim to eat small regular amounts. Seek urgent care if you cannot keep fluids down, sugar stays very high despite the plan, or you feel confused or breathless. Test urine or blood ketones if your care team has advised it.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: foot care
content: People with diabetes should check their feet daily for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling, or warm spots — nerve damage can hide injuries that then infect. Wash and dry feet carefully (especially between toes), moisturize, trim nails straight across, wear well-fitted shoes, and never walk barefoot. Any non-healing wound needs prompt medical care.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: A1C explained
content: The A1C test shows average blood sugar over the past 2-3 months. Normal is below 5.7%; 5.7-6.4% is prediabetes; 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes. Most adults with diabetes aim for A1C under 7%, but targets are individualized. A1C is checked every 3-6 months and is the best gauge of overall control.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: healthy eating basics
content: For diabetes, build meals around vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and lean proteins; limit sugary drinks, sweets, refined flour, and fried food. Consistent portion sizes and meal timing help steady blood sugar. Carbs raise sugar most — learning to count or balance them is the core skill. A dietitian referral helps most people with diabetes.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: prediabetes action
content: Prediabetes (A1C 5.7-6.4%) means blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet diabetes — and it is reversible. Losing 5-7% of body weight, 150 minutes of weekly exercise, and cutting sugary drinks cut the risk of progression by more than half. Ask about a repeat test every 1-2 years.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: diabetes and infections
content: High blood sugar weakens immunity, so infections (urinary, skin, fungal, gum) are more common and slower to heal in diabetes. Recurrent boils or urinary infections can also be a first sign of diabetes. Get any infection treated early; monitor sugar extra carefully during illness. Frequent infections or slow-healing wounds warrant a diabetes review.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Diabetes: monitoring frequency
content: How often to check blood sugar depends on treatment: people on insulin or with tight control may check 4+ times daily (fasting, before meals, bedtime, when unwell or exercising); people on lifestyle or metformin alone may check less often. Continuous glucose monitors provide constant trends. Follow your care team's schedule and record results for reviews.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: seasonal allergic rhinitis
content: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis) brings sneezing, runny or blocked nose, itchy eyes, nose and throat, worse at certain seasons or after exposure to pollen, dust, or pets. Relief: non-drowsy antihistamines, steroid nasal sprays, saline rinses, and reducing exposure (closing windows on high-pollen days, washing hair at night). Symptoms are usually worse in the morning.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: food allergy signs
content: Food allergy reactions typically start within 2 hours of eating: hives, itching, swelling of lips or tongue, stomach cramps, vomiting, and in severe cases breathing trouble or dizziness (anaphylaxis). Common triggers: peanuts, tree nuts, milk, egg, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish. Any reaction with breathing difficulty or faintness is an emergency. Skin tests and blood tests help confirm specific allergies.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: anaphylaxis action plan
content: At the first sign of anaphylaxis (breathing trouble, throat tightness, swelling, hives with dizziness, vomiting, or collapse) after an allergen: use the epinephrine auto-injector immediately in the outer thigh, call emergency services, lie the person on their back with legs raised (or on their side if vomiting), and give a second dose after 5 minutes if still severe. Never wait for symptoms to worsen. Anyone with a known severe allergy should carry two auto-injectors.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: antihistamines basics
content: Antihistamines block the histamine that causes allergy symptoms. Second-generation types (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) are once daily and less sedating. First-generation (diphenhydramine) causes drowsiness and is best for nighttime or itch relief. Take as directed for the season or exposure; antihistamines treat symptoms but do not cure allergy. Check for interactions with other medicines.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: allergy vs cold
content: Allergies cause itchy watery eyes, sneezing in bursts, and a clear runny nose that can last weeks, with NO fever. Colds bring sore throat, mild aches, sometimes fever, and usually last 7-10 days. Allergies recur in the same season or with the same triggers, every year. If symptoms last more than 2 weeks without improvement, allergy is more likely than a cold.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: allergic skin reactions
content: Allergic skin reactions — hives (raised itchy welts that move around), contact dermatitis (itchy red rash where skin touched the trigger), eczema flares — are treated with oral antihistamines, cool compresses, and moisturizers. Identify and avoid the trigger (new soap, detergent, cosmetics, plants, foods, medicines). Widespread hives with fever or joint pain, or hives lasting over 6 weeks, need medical evaluation.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Allergy: medication allergy
content: Drug allergies cause rash, hives, itching, or swelling after a medicine, usually within hours to days. Any breathing difficulty or swelling of the lips and throat is an emergency. Report all suspected drug allergies to every doctor and pharmacist — they can choose a safe alternative. A mild rash during antibiotics does not always mean a true allergy, so get it evaluated before marking it.

title: Allergy: when to see an allergist
content: See an allergist when symptoms interfere with daily life, are poorly controlled with antihistamines, you have had a severe reaction, or you need confirmation of triggers. Allergy testing (skin prick or blood specific IgE) identifies culprits so you can avoid them precisely. For severe allergies, discuss carrying epinephrine and, for some, immunotherapy (allergy shots) which can reduce sensitivity long term.

title: Asthma: what happens in an attack
content: In an asthma attack, airway muscles tighten, lining swells, and mucus increases, so breathing becomes wheezy, tight, and difficult. Triggers vary: allergens, cold air, exercise, smoke, infections, stress. Inhaled reliever medicine (blue inhaler) opens airways within minutes. Most asthma can be kept well controlled with daily preventer treatment, so attacks become rare.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: inhaler technique
content: Correct inhaler technique matters as much as the medicine: shake, breathe out fully, seal lips around the mouthpiece, press and breathe in slowly and deeply at the same time, hold the breath 10 seconds, then exhale slowly. With a spacer (for children and anyone struggling with timing), press once into the spacer then breathe in calmly. Rinse the mouth after steroid inhalers to prevent thrush.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: attack warning signs
content: Asthma attack signs: wheezing, chest tightness, coughing (often at night), shortness of breath, and needing the reliever inhaler more than every 4 hours or more than 10 puffs a day. Early action with the reliever inhaler and the written action plan prevents most attacks. If symptoms do not improve after the reliever, or breathing stays hard, seek urgent care.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: emergency signs
content: Asthma is an emergency when: the reliever inhaler is not working, breathing is very fast or labored, the person cannot speak full sentences, lips or fingertips look blue, or the person is exhausted or confused. Call emergency services and keep using the reliever inhaler (with spacer if available) every few minutes while waiting. Do not drive yourself to the ER during a severe attack.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: triggers to avoid
content: Common asthma triggers: cigarette smoke (including secondhand), dust mites, pollen, pet dander, mold, cold air, strong perfumes and cleaning fumes, exercise, and chest infections. Keep the bedroom dust-controlled, use hypoallergenic bedding covers, keep windows closed on high-pollen days, and avoid exercising outdoors in very cold air. Flu vaccination is recommended since infections trigger flares.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: preventer vs reliever
content: Two types of inhalers: the preventer (usually brown/orange, inhaled corticosteroid) taken daily to reduce airway inflammation — it works slowly and must be used regularly even when well; and the reliever (usually blue, salbutamol) used only for symptoms. Using the preventer properly makes the reliever rarely needed. Waking at night with symptoms or needing the reliever weekly means control is slipping — see your doctor.

title: Asthma: asthma action plan
content: Everyone with asthma should have a written action plan from their doctor: green zone (daily preventer, no symptoms), yellow zone (early signs like night cough or needing the reliever — double preventer as instructed and monitor), red zone (severe symptoms — reliever every few minutes and urgent care). Review the plan at every visit since control changes over time.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Asthma: cough-variant asthma
content: Cough-variant asthma causes a dry cough (often worse at night, with exercise, or in cold air) as the ONLY symptom, without wheezing. It is common in children. A persistent cough over 8 weeks, worse at night or with triggers, deserves evaluation — asthma is a possible cause and responds well to preventer treatment.

title: Medication: finishing antibiotics
content: When antibiotics are prescribed, take the full course exactly as directed, even when you feel better. Stopping early leaves surviving bacteria that can develop resistance, making future infections harder to treat. Do not share antibiotics or keep leftovers for later — each infection needs the right drug at the right dose.

title: Medication: paracetamol dosing
content: Paracetamol (acetaminophen): for adults, 500-1000 mg every 4-6 hours as needed, maximum 4000 mg per 24 hours. In children, use weight-based dosing, usually 10-15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours, maximum 4-5 doses per day. Never combine with other medicines containing paracetamol (many cold and flu products do). Overdose can damage the liver seriously.

title: Medication: ibuprofen vs paracetamol
content: Paracetamol lowers fever and pain but not inflammation; ibuprofen (an NSAID) also reduces inflammation, good for sprains, arthritis, and period pain. Ibuprofen should be taken with food, is not suitable with stomach ulcers, kidney disease, severe heart failure, or in late pregnancy, and is avoided under 3 months (under 6 months with caution). Paracetamol is generally safer first choice. Do not exceed either's maximum daily dose.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: Medication: missed doses
content: If you miss a medicine dose, take it as soon as you remember UNLESS it is nearly time for the next dose — then skip the missed one and continue normally. Never double up. For daily medicines, missing one dose is usually fine; for critical ones (insulin, blood thinners, epilepsy drugs, heart medicines), follow your care team's specific advice and mention missed doses at your next review.

title: Medication: storage and expiry
content: Store medicines in a cool, dry place (most in the bathroom cabinet is too humid) at the temperature on the label; some need the fridge. Check expiry dates regularly and discard expired medicines at a pharmacy. Do not keep unused prescriptions 'just in case'. Keep all medicines out of reach of children — lock them if toddlers are around.

title: Medication: side effects reporting
content: Any medicine can cause side effects. Report persistent or bothersome ones to your doctor rather than stopping the medicine yourself — sudden stops can be dangerous (e.g. steroids, beta-blockers, antidepressants). Seek emergency care for signs of a severe reaction: swelling, breathing trouble, rash spreading, jaundice, or unusual bleeding. Keep a written list of all your medicines and doses to show clinicians.

title: Medication: grapefruit interactions
content: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice interfere with enzymes that break down many medicines, raising their levels and side effects. Affected drugs include several statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), blood pressure medicines (nifedipine), and some allergy and psychiatric drugs. Check the leaflet of every prescription; when in doubt, avoid grapefruit while on regular medicines.

title: Medication: over-the-counter safety
content: Even OTC medicines have risks. Read the leaflet for dose limits and interactions; many cough/cold and pain products contain paracetamol — combining them causes accidental overdose. Avoid aspirin in children under 16. Ask the pharmacist about interactions with your regular medicines, pregnancy, breastfeeding, or chronic conditions before buying.

title: General: hand hygiene
content: Washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds — or using alcohol hand sanitizer — before eating, after the toilet, and after coughing or sneezing prevents the spread of most common infections. Cover coughs and sneezes with the elbow rather than the hand. This simple habit prevents more illness than any medicine.

title: General: routine health checks
content: Adults should know their blood pressure and get periodic checks: blood pressure every 1-2 years, blood sugar and cholesterol screening every 3-5 years over 40 (earlier with risk factors), and age-appropriate cancer screening (cervical, breast, bowel). Dental visits every 6-12 months. Tell your doctor about family history — it changes your screening plan.

title: General: vaccination schedule basics
content: Core vaccines: childhood series (measles, mumps, rubella, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, hepatitis B, HPV), annual flu for everyone over 6 months, COVID boosters, tetanus booster every 10 years, and for older adults shingles, pneumonia, and RSV vaccines. Check your local schedule with a clinic — timing matters for effectiveness.

title: General: exercise recommendations
content: Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise (brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of vigorous exercise per week, plus muscle-strengthening activities twice weekly. Any movement counts and small sessions accumulate. Older adults should add balance exercises. Check with a doctor before starting intense programs if you have heart disease or are very inactive.

title: General: healthy weight basics
content: Body mass index (BMI) is weight in kg divided by height in meters squared: below 18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 healthy, 25-29.9 overweight, 30+ obesity. Waist circumference adds risk information. Losing even 5% of body weight meaningfully improves blood pressure, sugar, cholesterol, and joint pain. Focus on sustainable habits — regular meals, vegetables, activity — rather than crash diets.

title: General: mosquito and tick bites
content: For mosquito bites: wash the area, apply a cold pack, and an antihistamine cream or tablet for itch; avoid scratching. For ticks: remove with fine tweezers close to the skin, pulling straight out without twisting; clean the area; watch for a rash around the bite or flu-like symptoms for weeks — those need a doctor (possible Lyme disease). Prevent bites with repellent and protective clothing in risk areas.

title: General: mental health first aid
content: Common signs that mental health needs support: low mood for over 2 weeks, loss of interest, sleep or appetite changes, anxiety that interferes with daily life, or withdrawing from people. Talking to a doctor, counselor, or helpline is the first step and genuinely helps. Self-care: regular sleep, exercise, sunlight, limiting alcohol, and staying connected. Crisis signs (self-harm thoughts) are an emergency.

title: General: travel health
content: Before travel: check destination-specific vaccine and malaria advice 6-8 weeks out, pack a basic kit (painkillers, antidiarrheal, rehydration salts, antihistamines, bandages, any regular medicines in original packaging), carry prescriptions for controlled medicines, drink bottled or boiled water where advised, and use repellent in malaria zones. Diarrhea that is bloody, with high fever, or lasting over 3 days needs medical care.
source: ClinicGuard curated demo guidelines (not medical advice)

title: General: smoking cessation basics
content: Quitting smoking improves health within weeks: circulation and breathing improve, cough lessens, and heart attack risk drops sharply after 1-2 years. Support doubles success: combination of counseling plus nicotine replacement (patches, gum) or prescription medicines works best. Cravings last only minutes — delay, drink water, distract. Repeated quit attempts are normal; each one is practice.

title: General: dizziness when standing
content: Feeling lightheaded when standing quickly is common (orthostatic hypotension) and usually harmless — rise slowly, stay hydrated, and avoid skipping meals. See a doctor if it causes fainting, happens with chest pain or palpitations, follows a head injury, or if you are on blood pressure or diabetes medicines. Dizziness with a new headache, weakness, or speech trouble is an emergency (possible stroke).
